content: ZMA, which stands for Zinc Monomethionine Aspartate and Magnesium Aspartate, is a dietary supplement commonly used by bodybuilders and athletes. It was developed by Victor Conte, the founder of BALCO Laboratories in Burlingame, California. The supplement is a combination of zinc, magnesium, and vitamin B6, and its formula is currently patent pending. The name ZMA is trademarked by SNAC System Inc., a company also founded by Victor Conte. ZMA is marketed with claims that it can increase testosterone and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels, which may contribute to improvements in muscle size and strength. It is specifically used as a bodybuilding supplement. The formulation includes two essential minerals, zinc and magnesium, along with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). These three components play critical roles in various biological processes. While studies indicate that most Americans consume adequate amounts of zinc and vitamin B6, over 50% of the population is deficient in magnesium. Engaging in physical exercise can lead to the depletion of vitamins and minerals, making supplementation particularly important for bodybuilders. This is due to increased blood sugar levels and urination during exercise, which result in the loss of magnesium, zinc, vitamin B12, vitamin B6, folic acid, and other nutrients. Although drinking water helps rehydrate athletes, replenishing water-soluble nutrients requires the consumption of fruit juice, sports drinks, or foods high in water content, such as vegetables. The typical composition of ZMA supplements includes 20–30 mg of zinc, 400–500 mg of magnesium, and approximately 10 mg of vitamin B6. According to the product's label instructions, ZMA should be taken on an empty stomach before bedtime, ideally two hours after the last meal and at least 30 minutes before consuming any other supplements. It is also advised not to take ZMA with calcium, as calcium can interfere with the absorption of zinc and magnesium. In a 1999 study conducted on NCAA football players during an eight-week spring training program, participants who took ZMA tablets demonstrated greater increases in muscle strength, free testosterone levels, and IGF-1 levels compared to those who did not. These findings were presented by Dr. Brilla, a sports performance researcher at Western Washington University, on June 2, 1999, at the 46th Annual Meeting of the American College of Sports Medicine in Seattle, Washington. This study was funded by SNAC Systems Inc., the patent holders of ZMA, and one of the study's authors, Victor Conte, has equity in the company. However, a subsequent study conducted in 2004 found that ZMA had no significant effect on strength or hormone levels. Despite this, the study did observe a reduced rate of muscle catabolism in participants and recommended further research to explore these findings.
